items.name: subobject; the preorder category Sub_C(X); inclusion and equivalence of subobjects
items.statement_summary: A subobject of an object X in a category C is a monomorphism m : M >-> X. A morphism between subobjects m, m' of X is an arrow f : M -> M' of the slice category C/X, i.e. an arrow of C with m' o f = m. These subobjects and morphisms form a category Sub_C(X). Because m' is monic there is at most one such f, so Sub_C(X) is a preorder. Inclusion is defined by: m is contained in m' iff there exists some f : m -> m'. Two subobjects are equivalent, written m == m', iff they are isomorphic as subobjects, i.e. each is contained in the other, equivalently there exist f and f' making both triangles over X commute.

items.name: equivalent subobjects have isomorphic domains
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered result stated and proved in the prose of Definition 5.1: if subobjects m : M >-> X and m' : M' >-> X are equivalent, witnessed by f : M -> M' and f' : M' -> M with m' f = m and m f' = m', then m = m' f = m f' f, and since m is monic f' f = id_M; symmetrically f f' = id_M'. Hence M is isomorphic to M' via f. So mutually-including subobjects have isomorphic domains.

items.name: a factorization of a mono through a mono is itself monic
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered result in prose: if m : M >-> X and m' : M' >-> X are subobjects with m contained in m', the mediating arrow f : M -> M' satisfying m' f = m is itself monic. Consequently M is a subobject of M' (not merely of X).

items.name: direct-image / pushforward functor i_* : Sub(M') -> Sub(X) along a mono
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered construction in prose: for a mono i : M' >-> X there is a functor i_* : Sub(M') -> Sub(X) given by post-composition with i, well defined because a composite of monomorphisms is again monic (and monotone for inclusion of subobjects, since Sub is a preorder).

items.name: local membership relation z in_X M for generalized elements
items.statement_summary: Definition made in running prose: given a generalized element z : Z -> X and a subobject m : M >-> X, define z in_X M to hold iff there exists f : Z -> M with z = m f. Since m is monic such an f, when it exists, is unique, so this is genuinely a relation (proof-irrelevant) between generalized elements of X and subobjects of X, not extra structure.

items.name: an equalizer as a subobject; its local membership predicate
items.statement_summary: An equalizer e : E -> A of a parallel pair f, g : A -> B is a monomorphism, hence a subobject of A, and it satisfies: for every generalized element z : Z -> A, z in_A E iff f z = g z. Thus E is exactly the subobject of those generalized elements of A on which f and g agree, i.e. E = { z : Z -> A | f(z) = g(z) } contained in A - the internalized comprehension of the equation f = g, generalizing the global-element description in Sets.

items.name: the poset of subobjects Sub_C(X)/== and Sub_Sets(X) = P(X)
items.statement_summary: It is often convenient to replace the preorder Sub_C(X) by the poset obtained by quotienting out the equivalence relation == (mutual inclusion); under that reading a subobject IS an equivalence class of monos into X. In Sets this quotient poset is isomorphic to the powerset: Sub_Sets(X) = P(X), i.e. every subobject is represented by a unique subset. Both readings of 'subobject' (a mono, or an equivalence class of monos) are used in the sequel.

items.name: pullback (fiber product) of a cospan
items.statement_summary: In any category C, a pullback of arrows f : A -> C and g : B -> C with common codomain consists of an object P together with arrows p1 : P -> A and p2 : P -> B such that f p1 = g p2, and which is universal with this property: for any object Z and arrows z1 : Z -> A, z2 : Z -> B with f z1 = g z2 there exists a UNIQUE u : Z -> P with z1 = p1 u and z2 = p2 u. The pullback object is also written A x_C B, with the mediating arrow written <z1, z2>.

items.name: pullbacks are unique up to isomorphism
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered result asserted in prose from the universal property: any two pullbacks of the same pair of arrows f, g are isomorphic; concretely, the arrows between them uniquely determined by the two universal properties are mutually inverse.

items.name: pullbacks from binary products and equalizers (both directions)
items.statement_summary: In a category with binary products and equalizers, given f : A -> C and g : B -> C: if e : E -> A x B is an equalizer of f o pi1 and g o pi2, and one sets p1 = pi1 e and p2 = pi2 e, then (E, p1, p2) is a pullback of f and g. Conversely, if (E, p1, p2) is given as a pullback of f and g, then the induced arrow e = <p1, p2> : E -> A x B is an equalizer of f o pi1 and g o pi2. (Proof by the two universal properties; uniqueness uses that the equalizer e is monic.) This realizes A x_C B as the subobject { <z1,z2> in A x B | f z1 = g z2 } of A x B.

items.name: products + equalizers imply pullbacks
items.statement_summary: If a category C has binary products and equalizers, then it has all pullbacks (of arbitrary cospans).

items.name: explicit pullback in Sets as a subset of the product
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered construction: instantiating the product-plus-equalizer recipe in Sets gives the pullback of f : A -> C and g : B -> C explicitly as the subset A x_C B = { <a,b> in A x B | f a = g b }, with the inclusion into A x B and the two coordinate projections as the pullback cone.

items.name: inverse image in Sets is a pullback
items.statement_summary: In Sets, for a function f : A -> B and a subset V of B, put f^-1(V) = { a in A | f(a) in V }, a subset of A, and let i : V -> B, j : f^-1(V) -> A be the inclusions and f-bar : f^-1(V) -> V the evident restriction of f. Then the square (f-bar, j, i, f) is a pullback: for all z : Z -> A, z factors through f^-1(V) iff f z factors through V. Hence the inverse image f^-1(V) as a subobject of A is determined uniquely up to isomorphism by being a pullback of the subobject V along f.

items.name: inverse image / reindexing map f^-1 : Sub(B) -> Sub(A) by pullback
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered construction generalizing Example 5.9 to any category: given f : A -> B and a subobject m : M >-> B, form the pullback A x_B M of m along f, with legs m' : A x_B M -> A and the map into M. Since m is monic so is m' (asserted, proof left to the reader as an exercise), so taking pullbacks along a fixed f defines a map f^-1 : Sub(B) -> Sub(A), m |-> m'. It is then announced as the goal of section 5.3 that f^-1 is a FUNCTOR, and hence respects equivalence of subobjects: M == N implies f^-1(M) == f^-1(N).

items.name: a pullback of a monomorphism is a monomorphism
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered claim: in the pullback square of a mono m : M >-> B along an arbitrary arrow f : A -> B, the opposite leg m' : A x_B M -> A is again monic. Stated in the text with the proof explicitly left to the reader ('Exercise!').

items.name: Two-pullbacks lemma (pullback pasting and cancellation)
items.statement_summary: In a category with pullbacks, consider a commutative diagram of two adjacent squares: a top row F -> E -> D over a bottom row A -> B -> C, with vertical arrows h'' : F -> A, h' : E -> B, h : D -> C. (1) If both squares are pullbacks, then so is the outer rectangle; consequently A x_B (B x_C D) is isomorphic to A x_C D. (2) If the RIGHT square and the OUTER rectangle are pullbacks, then so is the LEFT square. (Proof: diagram chase. Note the left-square-alone converse is not claimed.)

items.name: the pullback of a commutative triangle is a commutative triangle (prism lemma)
items.statement_summary: Given a commutative triangle over C - arrows gamma : A -> B, alpha : A -> C, beta : B -> C with beta gamma = alpha - and any h : C' -> C, suppose the pullbacks alpha' : A' -> C' of alpha along h and beta' : B' -> C' of beta along h exist. Then there exists a UNIQUE arrow gamma' : A' -> B' such that the resulting prism diagram commutes: the left-hand face is a commutative triangle (beta' gamma' = alpha') and the upper face (A' -> A, gamma', gamma, B' -> B) is a commutative rectangle - and moreover that upper square is itself a pullback. Proof: apply the two-pullbacks lemma.

items.name: pullback is a functor between slice categories: h* : C/C -> C/C'
items.statement_summary: For a fixed arrow h : C' -> C in a category C with pullbacks, pulling back along h is a functor h* : C/C -> C/C' between slice categories. On objects it sends (alpha : A -> C) to (alpha' : C' x_C A -> C'), the pullback of alpha along h; on an arrow gamma : alpha -> beta of C/C its value is the unique gamma' supplied by Corollary 5.11. The functor laws h*(1_X) = 1_{h*X} and h*(g o f) = h*(g) o h*(f) are verified by repeated application of the two-pullbacks lemma (e.g. for identities, stacking the identity square on the pullback square: the outer rectangle is a pullback, hence so is the upper square).

items.name: f^-1 : Sub(B) -> Sub(A) is a functor; it descends to the posets of equivalence classes
items.statement_summary: Let C have pullbacks and f : A -> B be any arrow. The square of categories and functors formed by f^-1 : Sub(B) -> Sub(A), f* : C/B -> C/A and the two inclusions Sub(-) -> C/(-) commutes, simply because f^-1 is by definition the restriction of f* to the subcategory Sub(B). In particular f^-1 is functorial, i.e. monotone for inclusion of subobjects: M contained in N implies f^-1(M) contained in f^-1(N). It follows that M == N implies f^-1(M) == f^-1(N), so f^-1 is also defined on equivalence classes, giving f^-1/== : Sub(B)/== -> Sub(A)/==.

items.name: characteristic functions, the natural iso 2^A = P(A), and substitution as pullback
items.statement_summary: In Sets: (i) the pullback E = { <a,b> | f(a) = g(b) } is the equalizer <f',g'> : E -> A x B of f pi1 and g pi2. (ii) Specializing B = 1, C = 2 = {top, bottom} and g = top : 1 -> 2, the equalizer is exactly the 'extension' of the propositional function f : A -> 2; so the correspondence between subsets U of A and characteristic functions chi_U : A -> 2 is rephrased as: U is the pullback of top : 1 -> 2 along chi_U. (iii) The isomorphism 2^A = P(A) sends phi : A -> 2 to its extension V_phi = { x in A | phi(x) = top } = phi^-1(top), described as a pullback. (iv) For any f : B -> A the inverse-image operation f^-1 : P(A) -> P(B) is given by pullback, and the two-pullbacks lemma yields f^-1(V_phi) = f^-1(phi^-1(top)) = (phi f)^-1(top) = V_{phi f}: logically, substituting a term f for the variable in a propositional function is modeled by pulling the extension back along f. (v) Hence the square with horizontal isos 2^A = P(A), 2^B = P(B), left edge 2^f (precomposition with f) and right edge f^-1 commutes; i.e. the isomorphism 2^A = P(A) is NATURAL in A, a strictly stronger condition than having an isomorphism at each object.

items.name: reindexing an indexed family of sets is a pullback
items.statement_summary: Let (A_i)_{i in I} be an I-indexed family of sets and alpha : J -> I any function; reindexing along alpha yields the J-indexed family (A_{alpha(j)})_{j in J}. This reindexing is a pullback: taking for each A_i the constant i-valued map p_i : A_i -> I and the induced map on the coproduct p = [p_i] : coproduct_{i in I} A_i -> I, the pullback of p along alpha is the reindexed family with its own indexing projection q; in symbols J x_I (coproduct_{i in I} A_i) is isomorphic to coproduct_{j in J} A_{alpha(j)}. Details are left to the reader as an instructive exercise.

items.name: finite products + equalizers iff pullbacks + terminal object
items.statement_summary: A category has finite products and equalizers if and only if it has pullbacks and a terminal object. The 'only if' direction is Corollary 5.8 (plus the terminal object as the empty product). For the converse, assume C has pullbacks and a terminal object 1: the binary product is the pullback over 1, A x B = A x_1 B; and the equalizer of f, g : A -> B is constructed as the pullback of <f,g> : A -> B x B along the diagonal Delta = <1_B, 1_B> : B -> B x B (intuitively E = { <a,b> | f(a) = b = g(a) } = { a | f(a) = g(a) }), the projection e : E -> A being verified an equalizer by a diagram chase.

items.name: diagram of type J, cone to a diagram, morphism of cones, the category Cone(D)
items.statement_summary: Let J and C be categories. A diagram of type J in C is a functor D : J -> C (objects of the 'index category' J written i, j, ..., their values D_i, D_j). A cone to a diagram D consists of an object C of C together with a family of arrows c_j : C -> D_j, one for each object j of J, such that for every arrow alpha : i -> j in J the triangle commutes, i.e. D_alpha o c_i = c_j. A morphism of cones theta : (C, c_j) -> (C', c'_j) is an arrow theta : C -> C' in C making every triangle commute, i.e. c_j = c'_j o theta for all j in J. Cones to D and their morphisms form a category Cone(D).

items.name: limit of a diagram; finite limit
items.statement_summary: A limit for a diagram D : J -> C is a TERMINAL OBJECT in the category Cone(D). A finite limit is a limit for a diagram whose index category J is finite. A limit is denoted by its projections p_i : lim_j D_j -> D_i. Spelled out, the universal property is: for any cone (C, c_j) to D there exists a unique arrow u : C -> lim_j D_j such that p_j o u = c_j for every j.

items.name: limit over the discrete two-object category is the binary product
items.statement_summary: Take J = {1, 2}, the discrete category with two objects and no non-identity arrows. A diagram D : J -> C is then just a pair of objects D_1, D_2 of C; a cone on D is an object C with two arrows c_1 : C -> D_1, c_2 : C -> D_2 (no commutativity conditions); and a limit of D, being a terminal such cone, is exactly a binary product of D_1 and D_2 with its projections. Thus lim_j D_j is isomorphic to D_1 x D_2.

items.name: limit over the parallel-pair category is the equalizer
items.statement_summary: Take J to be the category with two objects and two parallel non-identity arrows alpha, beta between them. A diagram of type J is a parallel pair D_alpha, D_beta : D_1 -> D_2 in C. A cone is a pair of arrows c_1 : C -> D_1, c_2 : C -> D_2 with D_alpha c_1 = c_2 and D_beta c_1 = c_2, hence equivalently just an arrow c_1 with D_alpha c_1 = D_beta c_1. A limit for D is therefore precisely an equalizer of D_alpha and D_beta.

items.name: limit over the empty index category is a terminal object
items.statement_summary: When the index category J is empty there is exactly one diagram D : J -> C, and a limit for it is precisely a terminal object of C; so the limit over the empty diagram is isomorphic to 1.

items.name: limit over the cospan index category is a pullback
items.statement_summary: Taking J to be the three-object finite category shaped as a cospan (two non-identity arrows with a common codomain), a limit for a diagram of that shape, i.e. for A -f-> C <-g- B, is exactly the pullback A x_C B of f and g.

items.name: category has all finite limits
items.statement_summary: A category C is said to have all finite limits when every diagram D : J -> C whose index category J is finite has a limit in C. Stated in running prose immediately after Proposition 5.23 to fix the meaning of its hypothesis.

items.name: finite limits from finite products and equalizers
items.statement_summary: A category has all finite limits if and only if it has all finite products and all equalizers; equivalently (via the preceding proposition relating pullbacks to products+equalizers) if and only if it has pullbacks and a terminal object. The proof constructs the limit of a finite diagram D : J -> C explicitly: form the two finite products P0 = prod over objects i in J0 of D_i and P1 = prod over arrows (alpha : i -> j) in J1 of D_j; define phi, psi : P0 -> P1 by pi_alpha o phi = pi_cod(alpha) and pi_alpha o psi = D_alpha o pi_dom(alpha); take the equalizer e : E -> P0 of phi and psi and set e_i = pi_i o e. A family (c_i : C -> D_i) is a cone on D exactly when phi<c_i> = psi<c_i>, so (E, e_i) is a cone and every cone factors uniquely through E by a morphism of cones; hence (E, e_i) is the limit.

items.name: limits of a given cardinality from products and equalizers of that cardinality
items.statement_summary: A category has all limits of a given cardinality kappa if and only if it has all equalizers and all products of that cardinality. Here C has limits of cardinality kappa means C has a limit for every diagram D : J -> C whose arrow-set J1 has cardinality at most kappa, and C has products of cardinality kappa means C has products of kappa-many objects. Proved by the same construction as Proposition 5.23.

items.name: dual theorem: colimits from coproducts and coequalizers
items.statement_summary: Dual of Proposition 5.23 and Corollary 5.24, obtained by dualizing cones to cocones and limits to colimits: a category C has all finite colimits if and only if it has all finite coproducts and all coequalizers, equivalently if and only if it has pushouts and an initial object; and C has all colimits of size kappa if and only if it has coequalizers and coproducts of size kappa. Stated without a separate proof, by duality.

items.name: functor preserving limits of type J; continuous functor
items.statement_summary: A functor F : C -> D preserves limits of type J when, for every diagram D : J -> C and every limiting cone p_j : L -> D_j, the image cone F p_j : F L -> F D_j is a limiting cone for the composite diagram F D : J -> D; briefly F(lim D_j) is isomorphic to lim F(D_j) via the canonical comparison. A functor that preserves all limits is called continuous.

items.name: representable functors preserve all limits
items.statement_summary: For a locally small category C and any object C, the covariant representable functor Hom_C(C, -) : C -> Sets (sending f : X -> Y to postcomposition f_* : Hom(C,X) -> Hom(C,Y), f_*(g) = f o g) preserves all limits. Proof reduces to products and equalizers: Hom_C(C,1) = {!_C} is a singleton; Hom(C, X x Y) is isomorphic to Hom(C,X) x Hom(C,Y) by pairing with the two projections; Hom_C(C, prod_i X_i) is isomorphic to prod_i Hom_C(C, X_i); and if e : E -> X is the equalizer of f, g : X -> Y then e_* : Hom(C,E) -> Hom(C,X) is the equalizer of f_* and g_* in Sets, since any h with f_* h = g_* h satisfies f h = g h and hence factors uniquely through e.

items.name: contravariant functor
items.statement_summary: A functor of the form F : C^op -> D is called a contravariant functor on C. Explicitly it sends f : A -> B to F(f) : F(B) -> F(A) and reverses composition, F(g o f) = F(f) o F(g).

items.name: contravariant representable functor Hom_C(-, C)
items.statement_summary: For a locally small category C and a fixed object C, the assignment X |-> Hom(X,C) is a contravariant functor Hom_C(-, C) : C^op -> Sets, sending f : X -> Y to the precomposition map f^* : Hom(Y,C) -> Hom(X,C) given by f^*(g) = g o f. Presented as the typical example of Definition 5.28.

items.name: contravariant representables take colimits to limits
items.statement_summary: Dual form of Proposition 5.27: a contravariant representable functor Hom_C(-, C) : C^op -> Sets carries all colimits in C to limits in Sets.

items.name: hom out of a coproduct splits as a product of homs (eq. 5.1) and its instances
items.statement_summary: Instance of Corollary 5.29: for a coproduct X + Y in any locally small category C there is a canonical isomorphism Hom(X + Y, C) = Hom(X,C) x Hom(Y,C), given by precomposing with the two coproduct injections (displayed as equation 5.1). Two consequences are drawn: (i) since the ultrafilter functor Ult : Bool^op -> Sets is representable with Ult(B) = Hom_Bool(B, 2), the ultrafilters of a coproduct A + B of boolean algebras correspond exactly to pairs (U,V) of ultrafilters with U in A and V in B; (ii) in Sets the same isomorphism is the exponent law C^(X+Y) = C^X x C^Y, of which the arithmetic law k^(m+n) = k^n * k^m is a special case.

items.name: reindexing (pullback) functor on slices of Sets preserves coproducts
items.statement_summary: For an I-indexed family of sets (A_i) and a reindexing function alpha : J -> I there is an isomorphism J x_I (coprod_{i in I} A_i) = coprod_{j in J} A_alpha(j). Read as a statement about the pullback functor alpha^* : Sets/I -> Sets/J, alpha^*(p : A -> I) = (J x_I A -> J), this says alpha^* preserves coproducts: alpha^*(A_i) = coprod_{j in alpha^{-1}(i)} A_i, and hence alpha^*(coprod_{i in I} A_i) = coprod_{j in J} A_alpha(j) = coprod_{i in I} coprod_{j in alpha^{-1}(i)} A_alpha(j) = coprod_{i in I} alpha^*(A_i). Continues an earlier example (5.15) that described reindexing as pullback.

items.name: pushout in Sets as a quotient of the disjoint sum
items.statement_summary: Given functions f : A -> B and g : A -> C, the pushout in Sets is constructed by first forming the coproduct (disjoint sum) B -> B + C <- C, then taking the equivalence relation ~ on B + C generated by the conditions f(a) ~ g(a) for all a in A, and finally taking the quotient: B +_A C = (B + C)/~. Intuitively B placed next to C with the images of A identified. Noted to be the dual of the construction of pullbacks from products and equalizers.

items.name: cocone, morphism of cocones, and colimit
items.statement_summary: Definition given in running prose, dual to Definition 5.18. A cocone from the base D : J -> C consists of an object C (the vertex) together with arrows c_j : D_j -> C for each j in J such that c_j o D(alpha) = c_i for every alpha : i -> j in J. A morphism of cocones f : (C,(c_j)) -> (C',(c'_j)) is an arrow f : C -> C' in C with f o c_j = c'_j for all j. A colimit for D is an initial object in the category of cocones, i.e. a cocone mapping uniquely to any other cocone from D; it is written colim_{j in J} D_j.

items.name: direct limit of a sequence of groups
items.statement_summary: Given a sequence of groups and homomorphisms G_0 -g0-> G_1 -g1-> G_2 -> ..., regarded as a diagram of type omega = (N, <=) viewed as a poset category, in Groups, the colimit G_infinity = colim_{n in omega} G_n always exists and is constructed as follows. Start from the disjoint sum of sets coprod_{n in omega} G_n and impose the equivalence relation generated by x_n ~ g_n(x_n); writing g_{i,j} = g_{j-1} o ... o g_i : G_i -> G_j for i <= j, the elements of G_infinity are classes [x_n] with x_n in G_n, and [x_n] = [y_m] iff g_{n,k}(x_n) = g_{m,k}(y_m) for some k >= m,n. The group structure is [x]*[y] = [x'*y'] for representatives x', y' in a common G_n, with unit [u_0] and inverse [x]^{-1} = [x^{-1}]; the maps u_n : G_n -> G_infinity, u_n(x) = [x], are then homomorphisms satisfying u_{n+1} o g_n = u_n. Universality: for any group H and homomorphisms h_n : G_n -> H with h_{n+1} o g_n = h_n there is a unique homomorphism G_infinity -> H commuting with all u_n, and it is even the unique such FUNCTION - i.e. the colimit is computed on the underlying sets, an instance of the forgetful functor U : Groups -> Sets creating omega-colimits. The same construction works for other equational algebraic structures (though non-equational conditions need not be preserved).

items.name: functor creating limits (and colimits) of type J
items.statement_summary: A functor F : C -> D creates limits of type J if for every diagram C : J -> C and every limiting cone p_j : L -> F C_j in D there is a UNIQUE cone pbar_j : Lbar -> C_j in C with F(pbar_j) = p_j and F(Lbar) = L, and moreover that cone is a limit for C in C. Briefly: every limit in D is the image of a unique cone in C, which is a limit there. Creating colimits is defined dually/analogously.

items.name: the forgetful functor Groups -> Sets creates omega-colimits and all limits
items.statement_summary: The forgetful functor U : Groups -> Sets creates omega-colimits (colimits of chains indexed by omega), and it also creates all limits. Stated as a summary of the construction carried out in Example 5.30; the same holds generally for categories of algebraic structures given by operations satisfying equations.

items.name: not all colimits of algebras are created by the forgetful functor
items.statement_summary: Counterpoint to Proposition 5.32: the forgetful functor does not create all colimits. The cited witness is that the coproduct of abelian groups has as underlying set the product, G + H is isomorphic to G x H, so the underlying set of the coproduct is not the coproduct (disjoint sum) of the underlying sets.

items.name: cumulative hierarchy as an omega-colimit, and its functoriality
items.statement_summary: The set-theoretic cumulative hierarchy presented as an omega-colimit. Basic form: V_0 = empty, V_{n+1} = P(V_n); since A subset B implies P(A) subset P(B) these form a chain empty = V_0 subset V_1 subset V_2 subset ..., and V_omega = colim_n V_n is the cumulative hierarchy of rank omega (continuable through higher ordinals). Relativized form over a set A of atoms: V_0(A) = A, V_{n+1}(A) = A + P(V_n(A)), with v_0 : V_0(A) -> V_1(A) the left coproduct injection and v_n = 1_A + P_!(v_{n-1}) : A + P(V_{n-1}(A)) -> A + P(V_n(A)), where P_! is the covariant (direct-image) powerset functor; then V_omega(A) = colim_n V_n(A), and V_omega = V_omega(empty). Functoriality: any function f : A -> B induces f_0 = f, f_1 = f + P_!(f), ..., f_{n+1} = f + P_!(f_n), whose squares commute, giving a cocone on the diagram V_n(A) with vertex V_omega(B) and hence a unique mediating map V_omega(f) : V_omega(A) -> V_omega(B); thus V_omega is a functor.

items.name: covariant (direct image) powerset functor P_!
items.statement_summary: Defined in running prose inside Example 5.33: the covariant powerset functor P_! sends a set X to its powerset P(X) and a function f : X -> Y to the image operation P_!(f) : P(X) -> P(Y) given by P_!(f)(U) = { f(u) | u in U } for U subset X. Contrasted with the contravariant (inverse-image) powerset functor used elsewhere.

items.name: omega-CPOs and continuous monotone maps
items.statement_summary: Defines omega-CPOs as an example of omega-cocompleteness in posets: a poset D is an omega-CPO if every diagram d : omega -> D, i.e. every ascending chain d_0 <= d_1 <= d_2 <= ..., has a colimit d_omega = colim_n d_n, characterized order-theoretically by (1) d_n <= d_omega for all n in omega, and (2) for all x in D, if d_n <= x for all n then d_omega <= x - i.e. d_omega is the least upper bound of the chain. A monotone map of omega-CPOs h : D -> E is called continuous if it preserves colimits of type omega, h(colim_n d_n) = colim_n h(d_n).

items.name: least fixed point of a continuous map on an omega-CPO (Kleene iteration)
items.statement_summary: If D is an omega-CPO with an initial (least) element 0 and h : D -> D is continuous, then h has a fixed point h(x) = x which is moreover least among all fixed points. Proof: define d : omega -> D by d_0 = 0 and d_{n+1} = h(d_n); since 0 <= d_0, repeated application of the monotone h gives an ascending chain d_n <= d_{n+1}, so the colimit d_omega = colim_n d_n exists, and continuity gives h(d_omega) = colim_n h(d_n) = colim_n d_{n+1} = d_omega (the last step because dropping the trivial first term d_0 = 0 does not change the colimit). If x is any fixed point then 0 <= x, and inductively d_{n+1} = h(d_n) <= h(x) = x, so d_omega <= x since d_omega is the colimit.

items.name: colimits depend on the ambient category: finite omega-CPOs in Pos versus in omega-CPO
items.statement_summary: An unnumbered worked example showing that a colimit is computed relative to the ambient category. Let omega_n = { k in omega | k <= n } be the finite omega-CPOs, with the continuous inclusion maps omega_0 -> omega_1 -> omega_2 -> ... In Pos the colimit of this chain exists and is omega. But omega itself is not omega-complete: the chain 0 <= 1 <= 2 <= ... has no colimit in omega. Hence the colimit of the omega_n taken in the category of omega-CPOs must be something else, and it is omega + 1 = (0 <= 1 <= 2 <= ... <= omega): in omega + 1 every bounded chain has its colimit in the bounded part and every unbounded chain has omega as colimit.

items.name: monic iff the identity square on it is a pullback; representables preserve monos
items.statement_summary: Show that an arrow m : M -> X in any category is monic if and only if the square whose two parallel sides are both 1_M and whose other two sides are both m (i.e. the square with corners M, M, M, X) is a pullback. Conclude that representable functors Hom(C, -) preserve monomorphisms.

items.name: monos are stable under pullback
items.statement_summary: Show that in any category, given a pullback square with vertical arrows m' : M' -> A' and m : M -> A over a map f : A' -> A, if m is monic then so is m'.

items.name: equalizers from pullbacks and products
items.statement_summary: (Equalizers by pullbacks and products.) Show that a category with pullbacks and (binary) products has equalizers, as follows: given f, g : A -> B, form the pullback of the diagonal Delta = <1_B, 1_B> : B -> B x B along <f, g> : A -> B x B, obtaining E with projection e : E -> A; show that e : E -> A is an equalizer of f and g.

items.name: the category Par(C) of partial maps
items.statement_summary: (Starred; partial maps.) For any category C with pullbacks, define the category Par(C) of partial maps in C: the objects are those of C, and an arrow f : A -> B is a pair (|f|, U_f) where U_f >-> A is a subobject of A (an equivalence class of monomorphisms) and |f| : U_f -> B is an arrow, taken up to a suitably defined equivalence of such pairs. Composition of (|f|, U_f) : A -> B with (|g|, U_g) : B -> C is defined by pulling U_g >-> B back along |f| to get |f|^*(U_g) >-> U_f and then composing, yielding (|g o f|, |f|^*(U_g)) : A -> C. Verify that this really defines a category (associativity and identities).

items.name: pushouts by duality
items.statement_summary: (Pushouts.) (a) Dualize the definition of a pullback to define the copullback, usually called the pushout, of two arrows with a common domain. (b) Indicate how to construct pushouts using coproducts and coequalizers, giving the proof by duality (dual to the construction of pullbacks from products and equalizers).
